item.title: The Party Wall Trap Catching Out London Landlords Mid-Renovation
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Renovating a rental property, particularly in London, can be an effective way to boost its value and rental income. Common projects such as loft conversions or extending terraced homes often yield significant returns. However, landlords may find themselves unexpectedly caught out by overlooked legal requirements, particularly those related to party walls.

What is a Party Wall?

A party wall is a shared wall between two properties, often found in terraced or semi-detached homes. Under the Party Wall Act 1996, homeowners planning renovations that affect these walls must notify their neighbours in writing. This includes work such as cutting into the wall, building on the boundary line, or excavating near neighbouring foundations. Failure to comply can lead to disputes, delays, and even legal action.

Many landlords prioritise structural surveys and building compliance when planning renovations but overlook the importance of party wall agreements. This oversight can result in costly interruptions mid-project, as neighbours may demand work to stop until proper notices are served and agreements are in place.

Avoiding the Party Wall Trap

To prevent delays and disputes, landlords might consider taking proactive steps before starting any renovation work. Firstly, it’s essential to identify whether the project involves a party wall or boundary. If it does, serving a Party Wall Notice to affected neighbours is a legal requirement. This notice should outline the proposed work and provide a timeframe for response, typically 14 days.

Neighbours can either consent to the work or request a Party Wall Agreement, which may involve appointing a surveyor to ensure both parties’ interests are protected. Whilst this process can incur additional costs and time, it helps avoid potential legal complications down the line.

Why Party Wall Compliance Matters

Ignoring party wall regulations can have serious consequences. Neighbours may seek an injunction to halt work, leading to costly delays. In some cases, landlords may also face fines or be required to rectify unauthorised work. Additionally, disputes can strain neighbourly relationships, which may be particularly problematic for landlords managing long-term rental properties.

By understanding and adhering to the Party Wall Act, landlords can ensure smoother renovations and maintain positive relationships with neighbours. Seeking professional advice from a qualified surveyor or solicitor may also be beneficial, especially for complex projects.

The Party Wall Act serves as a reminder that successful property renovations require more than just structural planning. By addressing legal obligations early in the process, landlords can avoid unnecessary setbacks and focus on maximising their property’s potential.

item.title: Estate agency challenges rivals over unauthorised property signs
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A local estate agency has called on its competitors to adhere to council regulations regarding the placement of unauthorised property signs. Kelly Residential, a family-run business based in Newton Mearns, has urged other agents in East Renfrewshire to comply with East Renfrewshire Council’s guidance on roadside advertising. This follows a council warning instructing estate agents to stop placing directional signs on public roads, grass verges, and street furniture.

A Push for Industry-Wide Compliance

Kelly Residential has publicly appealed to its rivals to follow the council’s rules, highlighting the need for a level playing field across the local property market. The agency claims it ceased using unauthorised signage immediately after the council’s warning but has observed that other firms continue to display such signs. This inconsistency has raised concerns about fair competition and adherence to local regulations.

To address the issue, Kelly Residential has launched a social media campaign to encourage industry-wide cooperation. The campaign, shared on platforms like Facebook and Instagram, aims to raise awareness about the importance of respecting council guidelines and protecting local neighbourhoods. The agency emphasised that its goal is not to target individual competitors but to foster a collective commitment to compliance.

The Impact of Unauthorised Signage

Directional property signs are a common tool used by estate agents to attract potential buyers to properties or developments. However, their placement must comply with advertising and highway regulations to avoid cluttering public spaces and potentially causing safety hazards. East Renfrewshire Council has made it clear that unauthorised signs on public land are unacceptable, yet Kelly Residential reports that the practice persists.

The agency has encouraged its competitors to review their signage practices and align with the council’s instructions. By doing so, estate agents can contribute to maintaining the aesthetic appeal and safety of local communities. Kelly Residential’s campaign underscores the importance of industry-wide collaboration to uphold standards and ensure fair competition.

As the debate over roadside advertising continues, homeowners and property professionals alike may wish to stay informed about local regulations. Adhering to these rules not only supports community well-being but also promotes a more transparent and equitable property market.

item.title: Land Registry proposes free access to property ownership data in major shake-up
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

HM Land Registry has unveiled potentially transformative proposals to expand free access to land ownership data while streamlining registration fees. The twin consultations, which could reshape how property professionals and the public interact with land records, aim to increase transparency whilst maintaining protections for residential homeowners.

Free access to land ownership data

Under the new proposals, individuals and organisations could gain complimentary access to comprehensive datasets revealing land ownership across England and Wales. The system would allow users to search mappable records showing who owns the majority of land parcels, potentially revolutionising planning and development research for professionals.

Currently, title register documents typically cost £7 each, requiring separate purchases for different properties. The reforms would eliminate these charges for bulk land data, though important limitations would remain:

  • Most residential properties would be excluded from the free datasets
  • Public sector bodies would retain full access to all records
  • Qualified researchers might obtain residential data for public interest purposes

The distinction arises because while most registered titles relate to houses and flats, larger commercial and non-residential holdings cover more land area. The proposals focus on making agricultural, commercial and undeveloped land ownership more transparent.

Simplified fee structure proposals

A parallel consultation addresses potential changes to Scale Two registration fees, which apply to various property transactions including:

  • Non-monetary transfers between parties
  • Below-market-value property transactions
  • Mortgage registrations

Currently calculated using property values, these fees may be streamlined to create a more straightforward system. HM Land Registry acknowledges the existing structure can create administrative challenges, particularly for complex transactions where property valuations may be unclear.

Property professionals and interested parties have until 20 March 2024 to respond to the land data consultation, whilst the fee structure review remains open until 17 April 2024. The reforms could significantly benefit developers, local authorities and community groups if implemented, whilst maintaining privacy protections for most homeowners.

As these consultations progress, industry observers suggest the changes could reshape land transparency in England and Wales, potentially influencing everything from local planning decisions to large-scale infrastructure projects.

item.title: Tesco enters landlord insurance market with new product launch
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Tesco Insurance has introduced two new insurance products aimed at private landlords and holiday home owners, marking its entry into this specialist market. The retailer’s insurance arm is now offering tailored cover for rented residential properties and second homes used for holiday purposes. This expansion builds on Tesco’s existing partnership with Prestige Underwriting, which will manage sales, customer service, and claims for these products.

Specialist Cover for Property Owners

The new products are designed to meet the unique needs of landlords and holiday home owners, offering protection that goes beyond standard home insurance. Landlords, for instance, may require cover for rental income loss or tenant-related damages, whilst holiday home owners might seek protection for properties that are vacant for extended periods or used by short-term guests. These policies are available online or via telephone, providing flexibility for customers to manage their insurance needs.

A Growing Partnership

The launch strengthens Tesco Insurance’s collaboration with Prestige Underwriting, a specialist provider in the property insurance market. Alex Cross, chief customer officer at Tesco Insurance, highlighted the importance of catering to customers with diverse property ownership needs. He stated, “For many homeowners, insurance requirements extend beyond their primary residence. Whether it’s a holiday property or a rented home, we’re committed to offering specialist cover that meets these needs.”

Tim Baxter, business development and relationship director at Prestige Underwriting, echoed this sentiment, emphasising the importance of understanding the specific risks faced by landlords and holiday home owners. He noted, “These property owners form a significant part of the market, and providing them with tailored insurance solutions is at the heart of this partnership.”

By venturing into the landlord and holiday home insurance market, Tesco Insurance aims to broaden its product range and cater to a growing segment of property owners. This move could offer homeowners greater choice and flexibility when securing cover for their rental or holiday properties.

item.title: BREAKING: Government publishes new rental property registration guidance for letting agents
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The government has unveiled fresh guidance for letting agents and property managers in England, paving the way for the introduction of mandatory rental property registration. This move comes as part of the Renters’ Rights Act 2026, which aims to streamline and regulate the rental market. Registration is set to launch in the West Midlands on 15 December 2026, with a phased rollout across the country concluding by November 2027.

What landlords and letting agents need to know

Under the new system, landlords will be legally required to initiate the registration process for each of their properties and pay an annual fee. Whilst landlords bear the ultimate responsibility, letting agents can assist by submitting certain details on their behalf. This arrangement, however, remains voluntary. Agents are being encouraged to engage with landlords early to discuss registration plans before the system goes live.

Key information that agents may submit includes details about houses in multiple occupation (HMOs), licensing specifics, tenant numbers, property furnishings, monthly rent, and included bills. Essential safety and compliance documents, such as gas safety certificates, electrical installation condition reports (EICRs), and energy performance certificates (EPCs), will also need to be provided. Agents will receive a unique access link for each property, enabling them to update records as needed. However, they must ensure the accuracy of any information they submit, as landlords will be notified of updates.

Strict deadlines and new advertising rules

The guidance introduces stringent deadlines for landlords and agents. Registration details must be submitted within 28 days, or the property’s registration will lapse, potentially placing the landlord in breach of their legal obligations. Similarly, any changes to property details, such as rent adjustments, tenant numbers, or updated compliance certificates, must be reported within 28 days. Agents can facilitate these updates using their access links, but landlords remain accountable for ensuring timely compliance.

In addition to registration requirements, the government has confirmed plans to mandate that properties must be registered before they can be marketed. Letting agents will need to verify both the landlord and property’s registration status before advertising. Property listings will also need to display two registration numbers: one for the landlord and one for the property itself. This measure aims to enhance transparency and protect tenants by ensuring only compliant properties are available on the market.

This new guidance marks a significant step towards a more regulated rental sector in England, offering clarity for landlords and agents alike. With the rollout approaching, those involved in the rental market may wish to familiarise themselves with the requirements to ensure a smooth transition.

item.title: ‘Tenants will pay the price’: Property commentators condemn landlord tax hike
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Property experts have raised concerns over the chancellor’s decision to increase tax rates on rental income, warning that tenants could ultimately bear the brunt of higher costs. The latest Budget measures, which will see tax on rental profits rise by an additional 2 percentage points from April 2027, have drawn criticism from industry analysts who argue it may accelerate landlord exits from the private rental sector.

Potential impact on rental supply and pricing

Estate agents and tax specialists suggest the tax hike could exacerbate existing pressures in the rental market. With private landlords already facing higher mortgage costs and regulatory changes, some may opt to sell properties or adjust rents where market conditions allow. Industry figures note this comes at a time when many areas already face significant demand-supply imbalances.

Darrell Evans of Lomond commented: “After a period of substantial regulatory reform, the market needed stability. This unexpected change risks reducing rental stock further, with tenants likely facing the consequences through higher costs or reduced choice.” Experts recommend landlords review their portfolios carefully, consulting both tax advisers and letting agents before making long-term decisions.

Alternative strategies for landlords

Facing diminished post-tax returns, some property investors might explore restructuring options, though these come with their own complexities. Amy Fry of Menzies LLP explained: “While transferring properties into a limited company structure might appear attractive, incorporation can trigger capital gains tax and stamp duty liabilities. Extracting profits from companies also presents its own tax challenges.”

Analysts note landlords could consider several potential responses:

  • Disposing of lower-yielding properties in their portfolios
  • Exploring rent increases where local market conditions permit
  • Diversifying into alternative asset classes with more favourable tax treatment

Madeline Gowlett of Travers Smith highlighted the growing disparity in tax treatment between property income and other investments: “With rental income now taxed at 4% above standard marginal rates, some investors may find share dividends or other assets comparatively more attractive.”

As the changes take effect over the coming years, the property sector will be watching closely to assess their full impact on both rental supply and pricing dynamics across UK regions.

item.title: £4.7bn first-time buyer scheme risks stalling housing market before it even starts
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The government’s new £4.7bn Your First Home scheme, announced in Chancellor John Healey’s Autumn Statement, has sparked debate among property professionals. Designed to assist first-time buyers in England, the initiative offers a government equity loan of 20% towards new-build homes, enabling purchases with deposits as low as 2.5%. The loans are interest-free for the first five years, with interest rates rising to 1.5% in year six and 3% from year seven. Whilst the scheme aims to boost homeownership, experts have raised concerns about its potential impact on the housing market and the risks it may pose to buyers.

Concerns Over Minimal Deposits and Market Impact

One of the main criticisms of the Your First Home scheme centres on the minimal deposit requirement. Housing market commentators have warned that entering the market with such a small deposit could leave buyers financially vulnerable, particularly if house prices decline. Negative equity, where the value of a property falls below the outstanding mortgage balance, could become a significant risk for those taking advantage of the scheme.

Additionally, analysts have highlighted the potential for developer fees to inflate house prices, reducing the affordability benefits the scheme aims to deliver. The limited reach of the programme, which supports an estimated 14,000 purchases annually, has also been questioned. This figure is less than half the annual rate achieved under the previous Help to Buy II initiative, raising doubts about its ability to make a meaningful impact on the housing market.

Potential Delays and Limited Scope

Another concern is the scheme’s April 2027 launch date. Experts suggest that this could create a five-month slowdown in new-build sales, as first-time buyers may choose to delay their purchases in anticipation of accessing the government loan. This short-term dip in activity could counteract the government’s goal of stimulating the housing market.

Furthermore, the scheme’s focus on new-build homes has drawn criticism for its potential to overlook the wider resale market. Estate agents argue that restricting support to new-build properties may limit the scheme’s ability to drive overall housing market activity. Anthony Codling of RBC Capital Markets described the initiative as “a catalyst, but not the catalyst we had hoped for,” noting that the funding level and scope may fall short of expectations.

A Missed Opportunity?

While the Your First Home scheme aims to address the challenges faced by first-time buyers, some commentators believe it may not go far enough. Charlie Lamdin, founder of BestAgent, described the initiative as having “the right aim, but the wrong answer,” emphasising the financial risks posed by low deposit requirements. The scheme’s delayed launch and limited funding have also been seen as missed opportunities to provide more substantial support to aspiring homeowners.

As the debate continues, it remains to be seen whether the Your First Home scheme will achieve its intended goals. For now, first-time buyers and industry professionals alike will be closely monitoring its development and potential impact on the UK housing market.

item.title: The property taxman cometh: Healey gives housing another going-over
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

The recent Budget announcement has brought significant changes to the UK property market, with measures targeting landlords, empty homes, and the Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT). These adjustments aim to balance government revenue generation with housing market stability, though their long-term impact remains to be seen.

Landlords Face Higher Tax Rates

One of the most notable changes involves increased tax rates on property income for landlords. From April 2027, basic-rate taxpayers will see their rate rise to 24%, while higher-rate and additional-rate taxpayers will face rates of 44% and 49%, respectively. This change excludes Scotland, where separate tax rules apply. The Treasury has described these adjustments as fair and proportionate, but landlords may view them as a significant financial burden.

The potential consequences of these higher tax rates could include a reduction in the number of private buy-to-let landlords. Many may choose to sell their properties, which could further decrease the supply of rental homes. This, in turn, might drive up rental prices, impacting tenants who rely on private rentals. Given that private landlords currently account for 19% of UK homes, compared to 16% in social housing, these changes could have far-reaching effects on the rental market.

Council Tax Premium on Empty Homes

Another key measure introduced in the Budget is a 100% Council Tax premium on properties left empty and unoccupied for at least 12 months. This surcharge aims to encourage homeowners to either occupy or sell their vacant properties, thereby increasing housing availability. However, the specifics of this policy, including exemptions for legitimate reasons such as property renovations or legal disputes, have yet to be fully clarified.

For owners of high-value properties, this measure could significantly increase financial pressure. While the policy intends to address housing shortages, its implementation will require careful consideration to avoid penalising homeowners who have valid reasons for keeping their properties vacant.

Stamp Duty Land Tax Remains Unchanged

Despite calls for reform, the Stamp Duty Land Tax (SDLT) has been left untouched in this Budget. item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property and mortgage landscape continues to evolve, with notable changes in leadership roles and team expansions across key industry players. Strutt & Parker has recently welcomed David Couch as its new head of valuation, following the transfer of residential valuation teams from BNP Paribas Real Estate. This move, effective from 1 October, integrates residential, mixed-use, and development valuation services into Strutt & Parker’s existing rural and residential operations.

Expertise and Expansion

David Couch brings over three decades of experience in the property sector to his new role. In today’s data-rich market, robust valuation advice relies heavily on the interpretation of evidence. Couch emphasised the importance of understanding local markets, assessing data reliability, and applying professional judgment to arrive at well-founded valuations. This approach aligns with the increasing complexity of the property market, where accurate and insightful valuations are crucial for informed decision-making.

This appointment is part of a broader trend of senior additions to Strutt & Parker’s rural business. Earlier this year, Natalie Gaibani joined as head of farming, while Ian Ashbridge strengthened the farm and estate consultancy team. Other notable appointments include Alice Rawdon-Mogg and Alastair Deighton in estate management, Mark Stephenson in minerals and environmental services, and Ed Vereker in building consultancy. With 20 offices across the UK, Strutt & Parker continues to expand its reach and expertise.

Previously overseeing land and development activity in North and East London, Davey’s expanded role will now see him collaborate with developers and investors across the capital.

item.title: Budget delivers further tax blow
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Chancellor's recent Budget announcement has introduced further tax changes affecting residential property investors, with private landlords facing increased taxation on rental income alongside limited incentives for the sector.

Key property tax changes in the Budget

Private landlords will see property income tax rates rise by an additional two percentage points from April 2027. This follows a previous two-point increase announced in November 2025, bringing the total rise to four percentage points over two Budgets. The new rates will stand at 24% for basic rate taxpayers, 44% for higher rate, and 49% for additional rate taxpayers.

Other notable property-related measures include:

  • No changes to stamp duty surcharges for additional residential properties
  • VAT relief on land sales to social housing providers
  • Additional funding for social and affordable housing schemes
  • £4.7bn government-backed lending for the Your First Home equity loan scheme
  • Removal of biodiversity requirements for qualifying brownfield developments

Industry reaction to landlord taxation

Property professionals have expressed concern about the cumulative impact on private landlords. Elliot Castle of Castle Property Group commented: "This is another nail in the coffin for a sector that's faced repeated tax increases and regulatory changes in recent years." He warned that higher costs might lead to landlords exiting the market or increasing rents.

Jennifer Lawler of Elite Realty Invest welcomed the prospect of regulatory stability but questioned whether the Budget would sufficiently encourage private investment in residential development. She highlighted the importance of private capital in meeting housing targets, particularly in regional cities experiencing economic growth.

Meanwhile, James Donohue of Landlord Property Exchange proposed stamp duty relief for tenanted property sales. He suggested this could help maintain rental supply by encouraging transactions that keep tenants in situ while providing immediate rental income for purchasers.

The Budget's measures continue the government's focus on supporting social housing while increasing taxation on private rental income, raising questions about the long-term balance between public and private sector roles in housing provision.

item.title: Damp or mould in more than half of PRS homes
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

New research has highlighted a worrying trend in the UK’s private rented sector, with over half of tenants reportedly dealing with damp or mould in their homes. A YouGov survey found that 54% of private renters are facing these issues, raising serious concerns about housing standards and the responsibilities of landlords.

The Extent of the Problem

The findings suggest that damp and mould are widespread problems in privately rented properties across the country. These issues can have significant implications for tenants’ health and well-being, as well as the condition of the property itself. Common causes include inadequate ventilation, poor insulation, and delayed repairs, which can exacerbate the problem over time.

For tenants, living in damp or mouldy conditions can lead to respiratory problems, allergies, and other health issues. Moreover, these conditions can damage furniture, clothing, and personal belongings, creating additional financial burdens for renters.

Landlord Responsibilities and Tenant Rights

Landlords in the UK have a legal obligation to ensure that their properties are safe, habitable, and free from hazards. This includes addressing issues such as damp and mould, which can be classified as Category 1 hazards under the Housing Health and Safety Rating System (HHSRS). Tenants who encounter these problems may wish to report them to their landlord or letting agent promptly.

If landlords fail to take action, tenants have several options available to them. These include contacting their local council’s environmental health department, which can carry out an inspection and enforce necessary repairs. In some cases, tenants may also be able to seek compensation through the courts if their landlord has neglected their responsibilities.

Preventing and Tackling Damp and Mould

Prevention is often the best approach when it comes to damp and mould. Landlords might consider taking proactive measures such as improving ventilation, installing extractor fans, and ensuring that properties are adequately heated. Regular maintenance and prompt repairs can also help to prevent these issues from arising in the first place.

Tenants can also play a role in reducing the risk of damp and mould by taking steps such as opening windows regularly, using dehumidifiers, and avoiding activities that generate excess moisture, like drying clothes indoors. However, it is important to note that these measures should complement, not replace, landlords’ responsibilities to maintain safe and habitable living conditions.

The prevalence of damp and mould in privately rented homes underscores the need for greater awareness and action from both landlords and tenants. By working together and addressing these issues promptly, it is possible to improve housing standards and ensure that rental properties are safe and comfortable for all occupants.

item.title: Over-30s account for four in ten HMO sharers
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Recent research highlights a notable shift in the UK housing market, with an increasing number of professionals aged 30 and above opting for house shares. Known as Houses in Multiple Occupation (HMOs), these arrangements now see over-30s accounting for nearly 40% of sharers, reflecting a growing trend among older renters seeking affordability and access to desirable locations.

The Appeal of HMOs for Older Renters

House sharing, traditionally associated with students and young professionals, is gaining traction among older demographics. For many over-30s, HMOs offer a practical solution to rising living costs, enabling them to save money whilst living in sought-after areas. With property prices and rental rates continuing to climb, sharing accommodation can provide financial flexibility without compromising on location or lifestyle.

Additionally, HMOs often come with inclusive bills and furnished rooms, reducing the hassle of managing household expenses. For professionals balancing work and personal commitments, this convenience can be a significant draw.

Changing Perceptions of Shared Living

The stigma once attached to house sharing in later life appears to be fading. As more professionals embrace this living arrangement, it is increasingly viewed as a smart financial choice rather than a compromise. The rise of purpose-built HMOs, designed with modern amenities and communal spaces, has also contributed to this shift, making shared living more appealing to a broader audience.

Furthermore, the social aspect of HMOs can be attractive to older renters. For those relocating to new cities or seeking companionship, sharing a home provides opportunities to build connections and foster a sense of community.

Implications for the Property Market

The growing demand for HMOs among older renters has implications for landlords and investors. Properties catering to this demographic may need to offer features such as spacious rooms, high-speed internet, and quiet living areas to meet their expectations. Investors might also consider targeting areas with strong employment hubs or vibrant cultural scenes, as these locations are likely to attract professionals seeking shared accommodation.

As the housing market evolves, HMOs are set to play an increasingly important role in meeting the needs of diverse renters. For over-30s, house sharing offers a viable alternative to traditional renting, providing financial relief and access to desirable locations. With changing perceptions and rising demand, this trend is likely to continue shaping the UK’s property landscape.

item.title: BTL investor losses rise a third to £1.1bn
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

Buy-to-let landlords across the UK reported combined losses of £1.15bn last year, marking a concerning 33% increase from previous figures. The challenging landscape of higher mortgage costs, shrinking yields and impending rental reforms has led many property investors to reconsider their portfolios.

Mounting pressures on landlords

The buy-to-let sector faces multiple headwinds, with rising interest rates significantly increasing mortgage repayments for those not on fixed-rate deals. Alongside this, operating costs have climbed whilst rental yields in some regions have softened. Recent government proposals for stricter rental regulations have added further uncertainty for landlords weighing up their investment strategies.

Industry analysts note these compounded pressures are prompting some investors to exit the market, particularly those with smaller portfolios or those heavily reliant on mortgage financing. The £1.15bn in reported losses represents not just paper losses, but in many cases the actual financial impact when properties are sold below their purchase price after accounting for costs.

Regional variations in performance

The pain isn't evenly distributed across the UK, with some areas proving more resilient than others. London and the South East have seen particular strain, where higher property values mean mortgage debts are larger and interest rate rises bite harder. Conversely, some Northern cities continue to deliver relatively strong yields, though even these areas face challenges from the broader economic climate.

Experts suggest landlords might consider reviewing their portfolios to identify underperforming assets. Options could include restructuring financing, adjusting rental strategies or in some cases, strategic sales. Professional tax advice is often valuable when considering portfolio changes, as capital gains and other tax implications can significantly affect the net outcome of any transactions.

Whilst the current environment presents difficulties, the fundamental demand for rental properties remains strong in most areas. Landlords able to weather the storm may find opportunities to strengthen their positions as the market adjusts to new economic realities.

item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The London Property Exchange (LPX) has announced a collaboration with the National Residential Landlords Association (NRLA), offering its 110,000 members access to exclusive off-market property deals and reduced sales fees. This partnership aims to provide landlords with unique opportunities to expand or refine their property portfolios whilst benefiting from cost-effective solutions.

What Does the Partnership Offer?

Through this alliance, NRLA members can access LPX’s platform, which specialises in off-market property transactions. These deals are not publicly listed, giving landlords the chance to secure properties before they hit the mainstream market. Additionally, members will enjoy discounted fees on property sales, making it a financially attractive option for those looking to buy or sell.

Off-market properties are often sought after by investors as they can present less competition and potentially better pricing. For landlords, this could mean securing properties that align with their investment goals more efficiently.

Benefits for Landlords

This partnership could be particularly advantageous for landlords navigating the current property market. With access to exclusive deals, they may find it easier to identify properties that meet their criteria without the added pressure of competing with a large pool of buyers.

  • Exclusive Access: NRLA members can explore off-market properties unavailable to the general public.
  • Cost Savings: Discounted sales fees could reduce overall transaction costs.
  • Streamlined Process: LPX’s platform simplifies property searches, saving time and effort.

Why Off-Market Properties?

Off-market properties have become increasingly popular amongst investors and landlords. These transactions often occur through private networks, allowing buyers to negotiate directly with sellers. This can lead to more favourable terms and a quicker sales process compared to traditional market listings.

For landlords, off-market deals can also provide access to unique properties that may not be available through conventional channels. This could be particularly appealing for those looking to diversify their portfolios or invest in specific areas.

The collaboration between LPX and NRLA reflects a growing trend towards specialised services tailored to the needs of property investors. By offering exclusive deals and cost-saving opportunities, this partnership could prove valuable for landlords aiming to maximise their investments in a competitive market.

item.title: First-time buyers face major monthly mortgage hit ahead of Budget
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

First-time buyers with smaller deposits are facing a sharp rise in mortgage costs, with monthly repayments increasing significantly over the past year. According to recent analysis, the average monthly repayment for a typical £250,000 mortgage over 25 years, at a 95% loan-to-value (LTV) ratio, has risen by £147 since November 2025. This equates to an extra £1,764 annually, posing challenges for those looking to step onto the property ladder.

Affordability Challenges for First-Time Buyers

The current mortgage landscape presents one of the toughest affordability environments for first-time buyers since the global financial crisis. UK Finance data reveals that mortgage repayments now account for an average of 22.6% of gross income for this group. This highlights the growing financial pressures faced by prospective homeowners, particularly those reliant on high LTV mortgages.

Whilst initiatives like the government’s proposed Your First Home scheme aim to assist buyers in accessing new-build properties with smaller deposits, experts caution that such measures alone may not be enough to address broader market challenges. Improving affordability and increasing housing supply remain crucial to easing the burden on first-time buyers.

Refinancing Concerns for Existing Borrowers

Higher mortgage rates are not only impacting first-time buyers but also homeowners approaching the end of fixed-rate deals. Analysis shows that the typical monthly repayment on a £250,000 mortgage over 25 years has increased by £131 since November 2025. This translates to an annual rise of approximately £1,572, adding further strain to household budgets.

Recent figures indicate that nearly 900,000 mortgages secured new deals up to six months before maturity during the first half of 2026. Experts suggest that more lenders should offer borrowers the option to lock in a new product six months before their existing deal ends, helping households better manage uncertainty around future mortgage costs.

Budget Speculation and Financial Decisions

With the Autumn Budget on the horizon, homeowners and prospective buyers are being advised against making rushed financial decisions based on speculation. Seeking professional advice and waiting for official announcements could help ensure more informed choices. Experts emphasise the importance of understanding the full implications of any Budget measures before committing to significant financial commitments.

As mortgage costs continue to rise, both first-time buyers and existing borrowers face mounting financial pressures. Whilst government schemes and lender flexibility may offer some relief, addressing affordability and housing supply remains key to improving market conditions for all.

item.title: New Land Registry rules set to change how property deals are reported
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Significant changes to land registration rules are set to introduce greater transparency in property transactions across England and Wales from April 2027. The new regulations will require disclosure of certain contractual rights that currently remain hidden in official ownership records, potentially affecting developers, investors and conveyancers alike.

What's changing in property transactions?

From 6 April 2027, HM Land Registry will require digital submission of information about specific contractual control rights affecting registered land. These include:

  • Options to purchase land
  • Conditional contracts
  • Pre-emption rights

Such agreements often allow developers or investors to influence land use without taking ownership, creating 'hidden' interests that aren't visible in current property records. The reforms aim to make these arrangements more transparent, helping potential buyers understand all parties with control over a property's future.

Preparing for the new requirements

Property professionals may wish to familiarise themselves with the new rules well in advance. HM Land Registry has published Practice Guide 84, which outlines:

  • Which types of agreements fall under the regulations
  • Who bears responsibility for reporting them
  • What specific information needs submitting

Conveyancers in particular might need to adjust their processes, potentially requiring additional checks and documentation for affected transactions. The Land Registry recommends firms retain relevant contracts and collect additional details such as dates and places of birth for individuals granting control rights. Where agreements affect only part of a registered title, spatial data may also be necessary.

Implementation timeline

The digital submission service will launch on 6 April 2027, with the first public disclosures expected from April 2028. This phased approach gives property professionals time to adapt while ensuring the new system delivers comprehensive information about land control arrangements that could influence development decisions.

While these changes primarily affect industry professionals, they may ultimately benefit homeowners and prospective buyers by providing clearer insight into any third-party interests that could impact a property's future use or value. Those involved in property development or complex transactions might consider reviewing the guidance now to understand how the changes could affect future dealings.

item.title: EYE NEWSFLASH: Property Industry reacts to Autumn Statement as landlords face fresh tax blow
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The Chancellor’s Autumn Statement has sparked mixed reactions across the property sector, with landlords facing fresh tax hikes whilst first-time buyers and affordable housing initiatives receive some support. The announcement, delivered by Chancellor John Healey, introduced a two-percentage-point increase in tax on rental income, raising concerns over the future of the private rental market and potential impacts on tenants.

Landlords Hit by Higher Taxes

The decision to increase tax on rental income has been met with criticism from industry experts, who warn it could accelerate the departure of private landlords from the market. Heather Powell, partner at Blick Rothenberg, described the move as “the final nail in the coffin” for many landlords, adding that combined with existing tax rates and restricted interest deductions, the sector is becoming increasingly unattractive for investors.

Greg Tsuman, Managing Director of Lettings at Martyn Gerrard, echoed these concerns, calling the additional tax “surprising and incomprehensible.” He highlighted that the move follows last year’s Autumn Budget, which already placed significant strain on landlords. With reduced supply and higher competition, tenants may face rising rents and fewer options, potentially pushing more towards corporate build-to-rent providers.

Support for First-Time Buyers and Affordable Housing

Whilst landlords grapple with higher taxes, first-time buyers have been offered some relief. The Chancellor confirmed the introduction of the Your First Home scheme and plans for a dedicated First Time Buyer ISA, replacing the Lifetime ISA. These initiatives aim to make homeownership more accessible for those taking their first step onto the property ladder.

On the broader housing front, £1.5bn has been allocated to boost social and affordable housing programmes. Land sold to social housing providers will also be VAT-free, potentially encouraging more development in this sector. Additionally, £430m has been pledged to support rough sleepers, helping them move off the streets and into stable accommodation.

Broader Economic Concerns

The Autumn Statement also introduced measures affecting the wider economy, including a £100 winter energy payment for households in Council Tax bands A to D, business rates relief for smaller firms, and an extension of the 5p fuel duty cut. However, the Office for Budget Responsibility’s revised growth forecast for next year—cut to just 1%—adds to the economic uncertainty.

Banks face an additional 3% tax surcharge, raising concerns that lenders may pass on higher costs to mortgage borrowers. This, coupled with the lack of significant changes to building regulations or broader housing market stimulation, leaves questions about how the property sector will fare in the coming months.

Whilst the additional funding for affordable housing and homelessness initiatives has been welcomed, the Autumn Statement’s impact on landlords and the wider housing market remains a point of contention. Borrowers and investors may wish to stay informed as these changes unfold, particularly those navigating the buy-to-let sector or seeking to purchase their first home.

item.title: Damp and Mould Reports: How Property Managers Should Decide What Happens Next
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Discovering damp or mould in a rental property can be a concerning issue for both tenants and property managers. Whether it’s a tenant’s photograph of a mould-covered wall or an unexpected finding during a routine inspection, addressing the problem promptly and effectively is crucial. However, the first step isn’t simply calling a contractor. Property managers may wish to consider the type of property involved and the potential causes before deciding on the next steps.

Understanding the Property Type

The approach to tackling damp and mould can vary significantly depending on the type of rented home. For instance, older properties with solid walls may be more prone to condensation-related issues, whilst newer builds might face problems due to inadequate ventilation. Understanding the property’s construction and design could help identify the root cause of the issue.

Additionally, the location of the damp or mould can provide valuable clues. For example, mould in bathrooms or kitchens often points to excess moisture, whereas damp in external walls could indicate structural problems. By assessing these factors, property managers might be better equipped to determine whether the issue requires minor repairs or more extensive work.

Assessing the Severity of the Problem

Not all instances of damp and mould are equal, and the severity of the issue can influence the necessary actions. A small patch of mould in a corner might be resolved with improved ventilation and regular cleaning, whilst widespread damp could signal a more serious problem, such as leaks or rising damp.

It could be worth arranging a professional inspection to accurately assess the situation. Specialists can provide insights into the cause and recommend appropriate solutions, whether that involves installing extractor fans, repairing faulty plumbing, or addressing insulation issues. Taking this step may help prevent the problem from escalating and ensure tenant safety and comfort.

Communicating with Tenants

Effective communication with tenants is essential when dealing with damp and mould. Tenants may not always report issues promptly, especially if they are unaware of the potential health risks or believe the problem is minor. Property managers might consider educating tenants on the importance of reporting damp and mould early, as well as providing tips on reducing moisture in the home.

Once an issue is identified, keeping tenants informed about the planned actions and timelines can help maintain trust and transparency. This might include explaining the steps being taken to resolve the problem and advising on temporary measures, such as using dehumidifiers or keeping windows open.

Addressing damp and mould in rental properties requires a thoughtful and informed approach. By understanding the property type, assessing the severity of the issue, and maintaining open communication with tenants, property managers can take effective action to resolve problems and ensure homes remain safe and habitable.

item.title: A Portfolio-Wide Approach to Drainage Maintenance for Property Investors
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

For property investors managing multiple rental properties, drainage maintenance often falls into the category of 'out of sight, out of mind' – until an issue arises. However, taking a portfolio-wide approach to drainage could help prevent costly emergencies whilst maintaining property values and tenant satisfaction.

Why Drainage Maintenance Matters for Property Portfolios

Separate drainage issues across different properties might seem isolated, but they often indicate gaps in a landlord's overall maintenance strategy. Blocked drains, slow-running water or mysterious damp patches could point to underlying problems with pipework, guttering or ground drainage. Left unchecked, these may lead to:

  • Structural damage from water ingress or subsidence
  • Health hazards from mould or sewage backups
  • Emergency call-out charges for out-of-hours plumbing
  • Potential disputes with tenants over living conditions

Investors with multiple properties might consider implementing a systematic drainage maintenance plan rather than addressing issues reactively.

Creating a Drainage Maintenance Strategy

A portfolio-wide approach begins with understanding the complete drainage picture across all properties. Key steps might include:

  • Compiling drainage records: Gathering any existing plans, maintenance logs or utility maps for each property to identify knowledge gaps
  • Professional surveys: Commissioning CCTV drain surveys where pipe routes are unclear or problems keep recurring
  • Preventative maintenance: Scheduling regular drain inspections and cleaning as part of annual property checks
  • Vendor relationships: Building ongoing relationships with drainage specialists who understand the portfolio

For larger portfolios, some landlords opt for digital systems to track maintenance schedules, prioritise jobs and store drainage maps centrally.

Long-Term Benefits of Proactive Drainage Care

Whilst implementing a drainage strategy requires initial investment, the long-term advantages for property investors may include:

  • Reduced emergency repair costs through early problem detection
  • Better preservation of property assets and capital values
  • Fewer tenant complaints and potential void periods
  • Simpler compliance with housing health and safety regulations

Like other aspects of property investment, a structured approach to drainage maintenance could help investors protect their assets whilst providing quality rental accommodation. With many competing priorities in property management, drainage might not always take centre stage – but keeping water flowing smoothly often prevents bigger headaches downstream.

item.title: Choosing Windows for Period Properties: Long-Term Costs and Value
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

For homeowners of period properties, windows play a crucial role in both the aesthetic appeal and practical functionality of the home. They influence everything from the property’s valuation and energy efficiency to its running costs and tenant appeal. However, windows are often treated as a maintenance task, with decisions based solely on the cheapest quote. This approach can overlook the long-term benefits of investing in high-quality, period-appropriate windows.

The Impact on Property Valuation

Windows are a defining feature of period properties, contributing significantly to their character and charm. Replacing original or period-appropriate windows with modern alternatives can detract from the property’s authenticity, potentially lowering its market value. Homeowners may wish to consider preserving or restoring original windows where possible, as this can enhance the property’s appeal to prospective buyers or tenants who value historic features.

For those needing replacements, opting for windows that replicate the original design could be a worthwhile investment. Specialist suppliers often offer bespoke solutions that blend traditional aesthetics with modern energy efficiency standards.

Energy Efficiency and Running Costs

Older windows can be a significant source of heat loss, impacting the property’s energy performance certificate (EPC) rating and increasing heating costs. Homeowners might consider upgrading to double-glazed or secondary glazing solutions that improve insulation whilst maintaining the property’s historic character. These upgrades can reduce energy bills and make the home more environmentally friendly.

It’s worth noting that listed buildings or properties in conservation areas may have restrictions on window replacements. In such cases, seeking advice from local planning authorities or conservation specialists is essential to ensure compliance with regulations.

Maintenance and Longevity

Period windows often require more maintenance than their modern counterparts, but their durability can make them a cost-effective choice in the long run. Regular upkeep, such as repainting and repairing timber frames, can extend their lifespan and preserve their visual appeal. Homeowners may wish to schedule routine maintenance to avoid costly repairs or replacements down the line.

When selecting materials, timber remains a popular choice for period properties due to its authenticity and longevity. However, alternatives like aluminium or uPVC can offer lower maintenance requirements, though they may not suit all historic homes.

Investing in the right windows for a period property can enhance its value, improve energy efficiency, and reduce long-term costs. By balancing historical authenticity with modern functionality, homeowners can ensure their property remains both beautiful and practical for years to come.
